title: Performance Evaluation of Sustainable C/L Strategies in Milling Carpenter® 20: Towards Green Manufacturing with Cryo + NF-MQL and Quenched Tool
abstract: Abstract Carpenter® 20, a Ni-Fe-Cr-based material, stands out for its exceptional corrosion resistance. However, its complex composition makes it difficult to machine due to rapid tool wear, high cutting temperature, and challenges in maintaining surface integrity. Optimizing machining strategies, particularly cooling and lubrication (C/L), is critical to ensure desired performance, surface finish, and extended tool life. Emerging C/L strategy, cryogenic (cryo) assisted nanofluid (NF) in minimum quantity lubrication (MQL) is gaining traction, which drastically enhances heat dissipation. Graphene (Gr) based nano particles (NPs) with high thermal conductivity, chemically inert, and low density were addedto the corn oil, which was used as an NF. This study focuses on milling of Carpenter® 20 with a quenched TiAlN-coated tool to assess the surface quality, tool wear, chip morphology, and residual stress with distinct cutting strategies (Dry, NF-MQL, and cryo + NF-MQL). The results showed that flank wear under cryo + NF-MQL condition was 0.163 mm after 2500 mm of cutting. Further, it reduces coating delamination, abrasion, and adhesion on both faces of the tool. The surface roughness was reduced by 46–48% (dry) and 9–12% (NF-MQL) in comparison to cryo + NF-MQL. Additionally, residual stress was analyzed on the machined face, which shows cryo + NF-MQL with a lower value of 336 MPa and 371 MPa with different cutting speeds.
journal: International Journal of Precision Engineering and Manufacturing-Green Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The automotive, aerospace, and energy sectors have become more interested in advanced alloys to support sustainable development goals and resource/system efficiency [ 1 ]. Carpenter® 20, known as Alloy 20, is a nickel, iron, and chromium-based austenitic stainless steel that has earned attention for its high corrosion resistance in chemical environments. Despite its incomparable characteristics, its unique composition leads to a lot of challenges in machining and hence calls for a thorough investigation into various cooling methods to optimize machining performance and tool life [ 2 ]. Vinothkumar et al. [ 3 ] highlighted the importance of attaining the required output performances while machining alloy 20 due to its high cutting temperature generation in the cutting region and tool wear [ 3 ]. Dry machining is not appropriate for high-strength materials in which high friction and temperature are developed. Nouzil et al. [ 4 ] mentioned that a proper C/L strategy is to be followed without compromising the sustainability of the environment and the materials involved. An investigation on the machining of AISI 4340 steel using CVD carbide-coated TiN/TiCN/Al 2 O 3  insert ended up with adhesion, abrasions, built-up edge (BUE), and chipping in tools [ 5 ]. In any metal cutting operations, cutting fluids (CFs) are widely used, predominantly for tool life extension, to act as an effective heat transfer medium, thus providing required cooling, to provide appropriate lubrication in the interaction region between the chip and the tool, and to flush out the chip from the cutting region. It is also reported that long-term exposure to these CFs leads to serious health problems like skin issues, respiratory problems, and other allied diseases [ 6 ]. The heat produced by moving parts and fluctuating outside temperatures can also affect the manufacturing process [ 7 ,  8 ]. As an alternative to dry and flood machining is MQL, also known as semi-dry processing, has advantages for the environment, worker’s health, and machining cost due to its low oil use [ 9 ]. When it comes to machining efficiency, MQL outperforms the dry method. Under low and moderate cutting conditions, the MQL system works well. Bedi et al. examined the application of rice bran oil (RBO) with coconut oil (CO) in the context of MQL machining of steel. It is observed that MQL-RBO outpaced MQL-CO, which exhibits lower cutting temperature, reduced tool wear, and better machined surface than dry condition when using an uncoated WC–Co (TTS 66 grade) tool. Additionally, studies have shown that under conditions of severe cutting, the MQL technique is unable to provide adequate cooling and lubrication (C/L) [ 10 ]. The distance of the jet primarily influences the area of droplet spreading in MQL. Additionally, the velocity of gas diminishes swiftly as the jet distance increases, leading to a significant decrease in the quantity of droplets that successfully reach the cutting zone. Consequently, reducing jet distance can enhance the lubrication effect [ 11 ]. Nanoparticles (NPs) are often used as reinforcement in oil to increase the C/L property because of their extraordinary physical-chemical qualities, which include great thermal strength, high melting point, and exceptional lubricity [ 12 ]. Padmini et al. used a coated tool to examine the effects of vegetable oil-based NFs on machining performance when AISI 1040 steel was being machined through MQL. Various NF samples were prepared utilizing nano molybdenum disulfide (nMoS2) dispersions in distinct biodegradable oils at different percentages of NP inclusion. Using CC + MoS 2  at 0.5% NPs inclusion reduces cutting forces, temperatures, tool wear, and surface roughness (Ra) by around 37%, 21%, 44%, and 39%, respectively, in contrast to dry machining [ 13 ]. Bertolini et al. studied machining trials on Graphene NanoPlatelets (GNPs) at different concentrations and flow rates. Initially, the properties of NF were examined in terms of coefficient of friction, stability, specific heat capacity, and viscosity. At different cutting lengths, the machined surface uniformity was examined, and the tool wear mechanisms of PVD TiAlN-coated carbide inserts were determined and measured [ 14 ]. Aydın et al. employed hBN/MWCNT, a hybrid NF-MQL, in the milling of Ti64. In comparison to dry cutting, hybrid NF-MQL reduces cutting force, temperature, carbon emission and enhances surface quality [ 15 ]. Su et al. analyzed the machining outcomes of Nanofluid composite electrostatic spraying (NCES)-assisted milling of aluminium alloys using various CFs. The combination of NCES with a commercial vegetable-based lubricant and graphite water-based NF exhibited exceptional lubrication performance, significantly lessening cutting force and temperature. This can be attributed to its remarkable charging and electro-wetting properties, along with the optimal graphite content [ 16 ].

Another environmentally friendly cooling approach that can be used instead of the MQL and NF-MQL method is cryo cooling, sometimes referred to as sub-zero cooling. Cryo cooling methods involve deploying liquid or gas coolants to the cutting area [ 17 ]. The most common cryogens are argon (Ar), Liquid nitrogen (LN 2 ), helium (He), and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) [ 18 ]. Once employed in the cutting area, the liquid phase of LN 2  instantly evaporates and spreads into the atmosphere, avoiding pollution of the environment. Typically, cryogens expand or evaporate, swiftly eliminating the heat produced in the cutting area. In addition to this, since it does not leave any residue, it eliminates the additional chip recycling process [ 19 ]. To study the performance of chip form and tool wear, Ravi and Gurusamy [ 20 ] milled tool steel using different cutting environments (dry, flood, and LN 2 ). When compared to previous methods, it was discovered that the cryo technique significantly improved the tool wear outcomes. However, the cryo technique doesn’t employ lubricants; they have a negative impact on surface integrity and tool wear because they increase friction in the cutting area, particularly at the cutting tool-W/p contact region. In light of this, researchers started employing hybrid C/L approaches (i.e., Cryo + MQL). The C/L qualities can both improve machining efficiency because of the hybrid approach [ 21 ]. Yıldırım et al. examined machining performance by exposing the Nickel alloy to MQL, LN 2 , and hybrid cutting (cryo + MQL) processes. The hybrid cutting method, according to researchers, demonstrated notable advancements [ 22 ]. Ti64 was machined using dry, wet, MQL, LN 2 , CO 2 , LN 2  + MQL, and CO 2  + MQL cutting conditions, and tool wear (Sandvik™ WC with TiAlN Coating) was examined by Sartori et al. [ 23 ]. According to the test results, the hybrid CO 2  + MQL cutting condition significantly reduced the tool’s crater wear. Gupta et al. examined the specific cutting energy (SCE) during the machining of Ti–3Al–2.5 V alloy utilizing environmentally friendly cooling strategies. Despite this, the investigation is also concentrated on the mechanisms of tool wear, surface roughness, and cutting temperature under hybrid cooling (cryo + MQL). The analysis of the tool wear rate indicates that dry condition leads to an increased formation of BUE. The hybrid cooling condition contributes to a reduction in the SCE during the machining of titanium alloy [ 24 ].

In addition to cryo + MQL, some researchers started exploring cryo + NF-MQL. Tool wear, temperature, and surface integrity were examined by Sirin et al. for the sustainable milling of Ti64 in various machining conditions. CuO-doped NFs produced better viscosity and pH measurements. The LN 2  + CuO hybrid C/L environment produced the best results in terms of key machinability outcomes, surface integrity, and tool wear [ 25 ]. Sarıkaya et al. investigated the machinability of Haynes 25 under various sustainable C/L techniques with PVD AlTiN-coated cutting tools. Experimental outcomes display that hybrid cooling systems, especially NFs with cryo CO₂, significantly improve the machining performance [ 26 ]. Figure  1  shows the authors who published articles in the fields of NF-MQl, cryo, and hybrid from 2020 to 2025. This search was conducted using the keyword “hybrid lubrication” in the Web of Science database. As shown in the figure, the hybrid system is becoming increasingly popular.
Fig. 1 Cryo, NF, and hybrid lubrication authors throughout the globe-2020-2025

According to previous literature, metal cutting operations are increasingly focusing on eco-friendly cooling methods. While research on cryo cooling, NF-MQ, hybrid machining, and other cutting-edge techniques has shown that it improves machining efficiency, surface quality, and tool life, it is still unclear how to determine the ideal parameters for cryo + NF-MQL. Research on the effectiveness of hybrid cooling systems in environmentally friendly industrial processes is still lacking. In addition to different cutting strategies, there is no evidence on the usage of coated quenched tools in the milling of Carpenter® 20 alloy with hybrid cooling. This study examines the effects of several cutting approaches (Dry, NF-MQL, and cryo + NF-MQL) on tool wear, surface quality, chip shape, and residual stress while milling Carpenter® 20 using a quenched TiAlN-coated tool. This study deliberately excluded MQL and cryo-LN 2  for comparison to emphasize eco-efficiency and sustainability because many papers were focused on MQL and cryo-LN 2  with different materials.

sections.heading: Machining
paragraphs: The experimental investigation utilised Carpenter® 20 as the primary material under this study. This alloy comprises an elemental composition of 32% nickel (Ni), 19% chromium (Cr), 0.06% carbon (C),2% manganese (Mn), 1% silicon (Si), and 2% molybdenum (Mo), with the remainder being iron (Fe). For the machining trials, W/m measuring 100 × 250 × 10 mm were employed. The experiments were conducted using a CNC milling machine, VMC 855 model, following the parameters outlined in Table  1 . Figure  2  presents the experimental setup and the measuring instruments used after machining. The input parameters were taken based on the previous research. In the milling operations, a BAP-07 H holder with a 10 mm diameter was used, paired with quenched carbide inserts (APMT113504PDER-FM) with a nose radius of 0.8 mm. The quenched inserts were procured from Vanbayes® Wuxi Bdex CNC, China. The reason for utilising a quenched tool because of its superior hardness in comparison to a PVD-TiAlN-coated carbide tool. The investigation conducted by Matei et al. [ 27 ]assessed the microhardness of the coated tool’s surface, revealing a measurement of 3187 ± 31 HV. The microhardness of the quenched tool examined in this study was determined to be 3700 ± 100 HV. Figure  3  presents the EDS mapping of the tool to confirm the coating elements and geometry of the tool. Each machining trial consisted of a cutting length of 250 mm, completed in 10 passes, using a fresh insert for every experimental run.

sections.heading: Cooling Conditions
paragraphs: The experiments examined the machining performance of Carpenter® 20 using dry, NF-MQL, and Cryo + NF-MQL methods. In this study, the Chenhai lubrication system (CH2000) was utilized for the MQL setup. The coolant, derived from Gr-based NF, flowed at a rate of 80 mL/h. The preparation of NF is elaborated in the following sub-section. The system operated at an air pressure of 6 bar, featuring a nozzle diameter of 2 mm and a distance of 50 mm from the nozzle to the W/m. Liquid nitrogen (LN 2 ) was selected for its effective cooling. Cryo LN 2  gas is taken from the cylinder through a pressure regulator connected to the cylinder to maintain a pressure of 2.5 bar and is flowed through a flexible hose via the nozzle exit.

sections.heading: Preparation of Nano Fluid
paragraphs: Distributing particles below a hundred nanometers in CF creates NF. When compared to traditional CFs, NF improved thermal characteristics and tribological performance [ 28 ]. NFs are frequently used in heat transfer applications, such as electronics, cooling systems, energy systems, and lubrication. The techniques used to prepare nanofluids are essential for achieving stability and even dispersion. The one-step method and the two-step method are the two fundamental preparatory techniques. The most popular technique for preparing NFs, particularly for commercial manufacturing, is the two-step process. Procedures, including magnetic stirring, sonication, and the application of surfactants, can be used to guarantee uniform dispersion and avoid aggregation [ 29 ]. The two-step technique was chosen for the creation of the NF in the current investigation because it was easy to use. Standard values for NPs inclusion ratio optimisation have not been defined, despite the existing literature on the subject. Studies published in the literature indicate that the ideal NPs inclusion ratio is between 0.5 and 1 vol% [ 30 ]. The preparation of Gr NPs based NF for machining follows a structured approach to ensure uniform dispersion, stability, and enhanced lubrication properties. Figure  4  (a) presents the preparation of NF. Gr NPs of 1 Wt. % was selected as the additive due to its excellent thermal conductivity and tribological benefits. The reason behind the selection of 1 Wt.% was because of previous studies, most of the researchers concluded 1 Wt.% as the optimal for preparing NF for machining [ 31 ]. To do machining sustainably, in this investigation, the same percentage was taken without doing any further analysis. Corn oil serves as the base fluid because of its biodegradable nature and superior viscosity. Table  2  presents the properties of corn oil. The preparation of NF starts with ultrasonication, where Gr NPs are initially dispersed in corn oil using a probe sonicator operating at a frequency of 20–40 kHz. The sonification process was carried out for 45 min, which helps to break down Gr NPs clusters and ensures a homogenous mixture by utilizing cavitation forces. A pulse is often employed to prevent excessive heat build-up. Following the ultrasonication, the NF undergoes magnetic stirring at a controlled temperature for 1 h. Magnetic stirring ensures even distribution of the Gr NPs throughout the base fluid. To improve the long-term stability and prevent sedimentation, a surfactant, Tween 80, was added. The surfactant decreases surface tension between the Gr NPs and the corn oil, improving dispersion and preventing particle settling. The well-prepared Gr NPs based NF is expected to significantly enhance machining performance by reducing friction and improving heat dissipation. Figure  4  (b) presents the instruments used for the preparation of NF.

Table 2 Properties of corn oil Density (at 25 °C) ≃ 0.92 g/cm 3 Viscosity (at 40 °C) ≃ 65 mPa.s Linoleic acid ≃ 57.8% Oleic acid ≃ 24.7% Palmitic acid ≃ 12.7% Stearic acid ≃ 2% Flash point ≃ 277 °C Fire point ≃ 340 °C

sections.heading: Nanofluid and Experimental Data Collection
paragraphs: Brookfield Rheometer DV3T measures the fluid’s viscosity at 25 °C at room temperature. Hot Disk Instrument TPS 2500 S is used for thermal conductivity post-experiment; each machined workpiece was meticulously cleaned using ethanol. Flank wear measurements were taken with the CUT801-4k tool measurement system. The Ra and topography of the end-milled surfaces were evaluated using a Zeiss LSM 800 Confocal Laser Scanning Microscope. Additionally, the morphology of crater wear, Vb end milling chips were examined using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) (Japan Electronics JMS-7610 F). The residual Stress analysis of the machined surfaces was performed using the PULSTEC µ-X360 residual stress analyser.

sections.heading: Mechanisms
paragraphs: Figure  5  (a) presents the illustration of NF-MQL and cryo + NF-MQL. The NF-MQL combines the principles of MQL with nanotechnology to enhance the C/L effect at the tool-W/m junction. In this system, a small volume of biodegradable base oil is dispersed with NPs and sprayed as a fine aerosol mist into the cutting region using compressed air.

The NPs suspended in the base fluid act as the thermal conductors, enhancing heat dissipation at the cutting zone. This prevents excessive temperature build-up, which is critical in machining, and reduced thermal softening leads to a more stable shear zone and refined chip morphology. The NPs create a thin, uniform lubricating film between the tool and the chip, significantly reducing the coefficient of friction. The rolling action of NPs further helps in lowering direct contact, minimizing tool wear, and improving surface finish. The presence of NPs repairs the micro-cracks on the machined surface caused by abrasive wear on the tool by the mending effect. In addition, it polishes and smooths the irregularities on the machined surface. Figure 5(b) presents the illustration of the viscosity of the NF decreasing with temperature. To maintain the viscosity of the NF and to provide additional cooling to the tool-w/m contact region, cryo can be introduced.

The combination of cryo and NF-MQL leads to controlled thermal gradients, uniform material flow, and enhanced share plane stability. The vital mechanism is that the cryo fluid freezes the oil + NP, preventing it from immediately evaporating from the contact region. Cryo cooling controls the bulk and tool temperature while the NF maintains lubrication and chip flow. This combined action results in minimal chip serration, reduced residual stresses, improved surface integrity, and prolonged tool life. Fig. 5 Illustration of NF-MQL and cryo + NF-MQL

sections.heading: Wettability analysis, Dynamic Viscosity, Thermal Conductivity
paragraphs: Performance and application are significantly impacted by the physical and chemical properties of the NF combination, including contact angle, viscosity, and thermal conductivity. Finding these characteristics contributes to the effective and optimal use of NF. A wettability test is carried out to understand how well the machined surface interacts with the coolant used and how the coolant spreads over the solid surface of the material. In this study, contact angle measurement was conducted for pure corn oil and Gr-enriched corn oil (NF) on a polished surface using the sessile drop method. The contact angle readings were repeated five times, and the average was taken as the final value. The corn oil exhibited a contact angle of 31.8º, and NPs enriched corn oil demonstrated a contact angle of 20.18º. This reduction in contact angle is attributed to the high surface energy of Gr and its strong interaction with the surface. The well-dispersed Gr NPs in the base fluid improve its spreading capability, allowing for more uniform and stable lubricant films during machining. A measure of a fluid’s internal resistance to flow is dynamic viscosity. It explains how easily a fluid can move or spread. For pure corn oil, the dynamic viscosity at 25 °C is around 38 mPa.s. When 1 wt% of Gr was added to corn oil, the dynamic viscosity increased to 51 mPa.s. The rise in viscosity is due to the interaction between the NPs and the base fluid molecules, which increases the internal friction and hinders the fluid’s flow. Adding more wt% of NPs in the base oil results in agglomeration and reduces the fluid flow. Thermal conductivity is the measure of the efficiency of the coolant to conduct heat efficiently. Maintaining a consistent temperature in the cutting area is crucial for achieving high-quality results. The thermal conductivity of corn oil measured at 25° C is around 0.152 W/m.K, which limits its effectiveness in high-performance machining applications requiring efficient heat dissipation. Gr + corn oil exhibited an enhanced thermal conductivity of 0.1834 W/m.K, reflecting a 22% increase over the base fluid. This significant increase in thermal conductivity is due to the promotion of efficient heat transfer through the Brownian motion mechanism. The NF with these obtained properties enhances the coolant’s ability to effectively carry away heat generated during the machining process, maintaining the machined part’s dimensional accuracy and mechanical properties, and preventing thermal damage to the W/m and the tool. Figure  6  presents the received values of contact angle, viscosity, and thermal conductivity after testing.
Fig. 6 Responses of Gr + corn oil, 1 wt% at 25° C

sections.heading: Tool Wear
paragraphs: One of the main indicators used to evaluate a W/m’s machinability is tool wear. It is dependent on the cutting environment, tool geometry, operating conditions, and the properties of the work and tool materials [ 32 ]. Tool wear has an indirect impact on energy usage and carbon emissions to the environment. Additionally, it negatively impacts the power needed for machining as well as the surface quality of the machined part. Tool wear is also categorized based on its location and pattern. Figure  7  presents the illustration of tool wear mechanisms. These tool wear types include notching wear, grooving wear, auxiliary flank wear, major flank wear, and crater wear [ 33 ]. The intense friction at the chip-tool junction is the primary cause of crater wear. High cutting speeds and the rubbing of flank faces against the W/m are the causes of flank wear and auxiliary flank wear. The outside end of the main flank has notching wear. This kind of wear is caused by mechanical contact between the main cutting edge and the hardened surface.
Fig. 7 Illustration of tool wear mechanisms at rake and flank side (modified) [ 34 ]

Flank side wear is characterized by a worn land along the flank face. The land width VB is the primary indicator and is further classified into VB C -wear at the rounded cutting edge, VB Max -maximum Vb, VB B -mean Vb, and VB N -notch wear. Additionally, the displacement of the cutting edge (SV α ) indicates the degree to which the tool edge has retreated due to wear.

sections.heading: Crater Wear
paragraphs: Crater wear occurs on the rake face of the cutting tool because of the continuous interaction of the tool and high-temperature chips [ 35 ]. It is influenced by multiple wear mechanisms as discussed in the previous section. Figure  8  presents the SEM images of crater side wear under distinct cutting strategies. Under dry condition, excessive heat was generated at the tool-W/m junction. At lower Vc (45 m/min), moderate crater wear was observed compared to the higher Vc. Continuous contact between the tool and the hot chips led to severe adhesion of W/m onto the tool surface [ 36 ]. This adhesion caused micro-welding, which later resulted in material pull-out (chipping) from the tool, which accelerates the wear. At the higher Vc (60 m/min), significant nose damage and severe crater were seen. An increase in friction and thermal energy weakens the coating and leads to coating delamination. The non-presence of a cooling medium resulted in excessive thermal softening of the tool material, reducing its wear resistance. Dry cutting environment causes high stress concentration, which leads to eventual chipping of the tool edge [ 37 ]. The application of NF-MQL improved the L/C properties during milling. At a Vc of 45 m/min, crater wear was reduced compared to dry cutting condition, as the NF provided an effective barrier against direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby minimizing adhesion. However, at a Vc of 60 m/min, the wear mechanisms slightly intensified as a reason of increased thermal load. The presence of NF helped in reducing tool-chip friction, but localized heating still led to coating delamination. At higher Vc, adhesion of material from the W/m led to minor chipping. However, the Gr-based L/C effectively minimized tool wear progression by enhancing chip evacuation, thereby decreasing the intensity of wear. Cryo + NF-MQL provided the best result in reducing the crater wear. Under Cryo + NF-MQL, the combination of C/L created a synergistic effect, improving the wear resistance and tool life. The rapid cooling by LN 2  prevented the thermal expansion and contraction cycles, which are often responsible for coating delamination. Further, enhanced lubrication by the NF in connection with cryo LN 2  led to smoother chip flow and lowered thermal concentration on the tool. Sarikaya et al. noted a similar result but with a different cryo fluid [ 38 ]. Another important observation was the suppression of chipping due to the reduced brittleness of the TiAlN coating at lower temperatures.
Fig. 8 Crater wear under distinct cutting strategies
Fig. 9 EDS elemental Mapping for crater side at a Vc of 60 m/min and a  fr  of 200 mm/min under different cutting environments

Figure  9  presents the EDS elemental mapping on the crater side at a Vc of 60 m/min and a  fr  of 200 mm/min under different cutting environments. Elemental analysis on the crater region revealed a notable variation in the presence of W/m, specifically Fe, Ni, and Cr, in addition to the tool coating and substrate. Under dry cutting, wt% of Fe (9.87), Ni (7.49), and Cr (6.12) were observed. This is primarily due to the thermo-chemical interaction between the tool and W/m. The high thermal load softens the tool surface and accelerates atomic interdiffusion, thereby embedding W/m elements in the crater region along with coating and substrate. By the introduction of NF-MQL, crater wear was reduced significantly (Fe-4.18 wt%, Ni-5.73 wt%, and Cr-2.42 wt%). The lubricant reduces the direct asperity contact and lowers the temperature at the cutting region. This lessens the severity of crater wear and suppresses the diffusion of W/m elements into the tool material. Cryo + NF-MQL condition demonstrated the best performance with a minimal trace of Fe (2.9 wt%), Ni (1.8 wt%), and Cr (1.1 wt%). The combined effect of NF lubrication and cryo cooling maintains a stable cutting environment and prevents material transfer from the W/m to the tool’s surface.

sections.heading: Flank Wear
paragraphs: Wear on the flank side is mainly due to the cutting environment and its effect on the tool-W/m contact region. The high cutting heat produced due to continuous rubbing accelerates material softening, reducing the hardness of the tool at the contact region [ 39 ]. Figure  10  (a-d) presents the Vb under varied Vc and magnified values from 1500 to 2500 mm LOC under distinct environmental conditions. The Vb results reveal a clear dependence of both Vc and cutting environments. At a Vc of 45 m/min, the wear under dry condition increased and reached 0.312 mm at 1750 cutting length. Extreme temperature load accelerates tool softening and diffusion wear, especially at the flank side, where continuous rubbing occurs. A similar trend was observed at 60 m/min, where higher Vc naturally generates more heat, leading to a greater Vb of 0.329 under dry condition. NF-MQL significantly lessens the wear, with VB reaching 0.194 mm at 45 m/min and 0.204 mm at 60 m/min, of 2500 mm LOC. The NF in MQL enhances the heat transfer due to their superior thermal conductivity and provides a layer of lubricating film that reduces tool-W/m contact. The cryo-NF-MQL condition showed a remarkable improvement in limiting Vb to 0.1552 at 45 m/min with the same LOC (2500 mm). The cryo LN 2  environment rapidly absorbs the produced heat at the cutting region and enhances lubrication by NF-MQL, maintaining the tool at a lower temperature and thus preserving the hardness of the tool. The same trend was seen when the Vc was increased to 60 m/min, resulting in a Vb of 0.163 mm. Cryo-NF-MQL lessens the Vb by 20% at both the Vc’s in contrast to NF-MQL. The enhanced C/L significantly removed heat and reduced the dominant wear mechanisms. In his research, Mehmet et al. confirmed that with the cryo + NF-MQL condition, there has been a notable decrease in Vb [ 40 ].

Fig. 10 ( a ) Vb at 45 m/min, ( b ) magnified image from 1500–2500 mm LOC at 45 m/ min; ( c ) Vb at 60 m/min, ( d ) magnified image from 1500–2500 mm LOC at 60 m/ min under varied cutting environments
Fig. 11 Flank wear under distinct cutting strategies
Fig. 12 EDS elemental Mapping for flank side at a Vc of 60 m/min and a  fr  of 200 mm/min under different cutting environments

Figure  11  presents the SEM images of the flank side under distinct cutting strategies. At 60 m/min, the wear significantly increased, leading to noticeable nose damage; this damage is also seen in the crater side of the tool. The combination of thermal softening, abrasive plowing, and intermittent adhesion led to severe material loss along the tool flank, reducing tool life and surface finish quality. The introduction of NF-MQL provided enhanced L/C, reducing abrasive wear seen under dry condition. The Gr-based NF reduces the direct contact between the tool and the W/m, thereby limiting the abrasion. The reduction of heat development in the contact region produces smoother chips. At higher Vc (60 m/min), the presence of NF in the contact region reduces BUE formation, but high cutting forces at the elevated speed promoted adhesion along the cutting tip. NF-MQL outperformed dry condition by limiting abrasion. Under the cryo + NF-MQL condition, the Vb was minimal, as the hardened tool surface experienced lower thermal and mechanical stresses. At 60 m/min, the Vb was still present but significantly lower than in the other conditions. The combined effect of both the coolants prevents adhesion at a higher level by providing proper C/L.

Figure  12  presents the EDS elemental mapping on the flank side at a Vc of 60 m/min and a  fr  of 200 mm/min under different cutting environments. In the flank region, the highest elemental deposition of W/m is observed under the NF-MQL condition (Fe-14.02 wt%, Ni-11.31wt.%, Cr-6.17wt.%). This higher presence is attributed to the localized thermal softening at the tool-W/m junction. While NF-MQL provides lubrication, it may not sufficiently cool the flank face, where continuous rubbing occurs between the tool and the freshly machined surface. The resulting temperature rise leads to adhesion and smearing of this softened W/m onto the tool. In contrast, the dry condition shows moderate diffusion (Fe-6.03 wt%, Ni-4.15 wt%, Cr-2.24 wt%) of W/m because the adhered material in the nose area is removed due to thermo-mechanical load. The cryo + NF-MQL condition exhibits the lowest elemental transfer (Fe-2.14 wt%, Ni-1.22 wt%, Cr-0.85 wt%). The Superior C/L assistance, which maintains a lower temperature, minimizes adhesive wear and significantly restricts the diffusion and sticking off W/m onto the tool flank face.

sections.heading: Surface Roughness
paragraphs: Figure  14  presents the variation of Ra under different cutting environments and speeds. The average Ra of three measured values at different places of the machined faces was taken for discussion in this section. Under dry condition, the highest average Ra of 2.35 μm at 45 m/min and 2.22 μm at 60 m/min. This is primarily due to the non-presence of lubrication, which results in increased friction at the tool-W/m junction. This elevated friction contributed to tool damage, which adversely affects the surface quality [ 41 ]. At a higher Vc of 60 m/min, a decrease in Ra was noted, which is likely due to the thermal softening of the material, which made it easier to shear. Under NF-MQL, Ra significantly improved, with Ra values dropping to 1.36 μm (45 m/min) and 1.30 μm (60 m/min). This improvement is due to the enhanced C/L property of the NF. The suspended Gr increases the fluid’s thermal conductivity and forms a protective tribo-film on the tool surface [ 12 ]. Reduction of friction suppresses BUE and promotes a more stable cutting process. The slight improvement of Ra at a Vc of 60 m/min was due to the combined effect of Gr-induced lubrication, which improved chip flow and helped to refine the surface even further. The quality surface was achieved under cryo + NF-MQL, with Ra values as low as 1.24 μm at 45 m/min and 1.15 μm at 60 m/min. This notable enhancement is due to the synergistic action of cryo-cooling and NF-MQL lubrication. The cryo coolant effectively maintains a significantly low cutting temperature, which helps to prevent blunt cuts and consequently leads to a marked reduction in Ra. Nonetheless, NF demonstrates exceptional heat dissipation properties, significantly enhancing the retention of the tool’s hardness. This mitigates the possibility of significant welding of the tool flank side to the W/p, consequently improving the surface quality [ 42 ].
Fig. 13 Illustration of average surface roughness

Figure  15  presents the 2D and 3D topography of the machined face under distinct cutting environments. The cutting conditions were employed to evaluate the influence of surface topography, specifically through the Sa (arithmetic mean height) parameter. The results showed a progressive improvement in surface finish across conditions, with a Sa value recorded at 1.79 μm for dry, 1.08 μm for NF-MQL, and 0.73 μm for cryo + NF-MQL. Under the dry cutting strategy, the highest Sa value reflects an intense tool-W/m interaction. The non-presence of coolant creates a rough surface. Next comes NF-MQL, the Sa value reduced to 1.08 μm, indicating a better surface profile compared to dry cutting. The improvement is because of the consistent shearing of W/m from the cutting region [ 43 ]. The optimal surface was produced under cryo + NF-MQL condition, which is less than 1.00 μm. The combined effect of both the coolants from the different nozzles is the reason behind the enhancement in surface finish.

sections.heading: Chip Morphology
paragraphs: The morphology of the chips generated during the machining of Carpenter® 20 was significantly influenced by the cooling strategy and tool-W/m interaction. Figure  16  presents the chip morphology at a Vc of 60 m/min and a  fr  of 200 mm/min under different cutting environments. Under dry machining condition, the chips exhibited uneven serration because of high cutting temperature, elevated strain rate, and the absence of C/L. These conditions promote unstable shear localization and periodic material tearing during chip formation. The average chip thickness (T1, T2, and T3) was measured at three random locations of the chip. The dry condition shows the highest of 736.27 μm, indicating excessive plastic deformation and material bulging due to intense thermal softening. When NF-MQL was employed, a noticeable improvement in chip morphology was observed. The chips formed under NF-MQL showed moderate serration. This C/L combination lowered the cutting region heat and friction, allowing for more consistent plastic flow during chip formation. The resulting average chip thickness decreased to 720.40 μm, reflecting improved material control and less severe deformation. The most refined chip structure was obtained with cryo + NF-MQL, which yielded evenly serrated chips with minimal fluctuation in chip profile. The cryo environment effectively reduced the cutting heat, minimizing thermal softening and stabilizing the shear zone [ 44 ]. As a result, chip segmentation was more controlled, and the deformation layer became thinner and more uniform. The average chip thickness in this condition was the lowest recorded at 711.13 μm, highlighting the enhanced chip breakability and dimensional consistency. The use of quenched carbide cutting tools further contributed to maintaining tool hardness at elevated loads, supporting more predictable chip formation across varied cutting environments.

sections.heading: Residual Stress
paragraphs: Fig. 17 Illustration of residual stress formation (modified) [ 46 ]

Figure  18  presents the variation of residual stress under different cutting environments and speeds. In dry condition, excessive heat generation at the tool-W/m junction results in steep thermal gradients and localized plastic deformation [ 47 ]. This condition induces tensile residual stress on the machined face (729 MPa at 45 m/min and 766 MPa at 60 m/min), which is undesirable as it can promote crack initiation and propagate fatigue failure. From the residual stress results, it is understood that, on the microstructural level, dry condition tends to cause grain coarsening, elevated dislocation densities, and thermal softening on the surface [ 48 ]. The microstructural changes negatively affect surface integrity, producing a mechanically unstable and thermally damaged surface layer. The usage of NF-MQL significantly lessens the residual stress (531 MPa at 45 m/min and 559 MPa at 60 m/min). The better C/L property of NF-MQL moderates the heat input, controls the strain localization, and results in more uniform plastic deformation. As a result, the surface microstructure remains more refined, with less thermal alteration, leading to improved surface integrity characterized by smoother surface finish, lower microcrack susceptibility, and reduction in tensile stress magnitude. The cryo + NF-MQL further reduced the residual stresses to 336 MPa at 45 m/min and 371 MPa at 60 m/min. Cryo + NF-MQL at the cutting area rapidly removes heat from the cutting area, significantly suppressing thermal-induced defects and microstructural transformations. The rapid cooling by cryo LN 2  [ 49 ] and lubrication by NF-MQL [ 50 ] lead to grain refinement by suppressing recrystallization and limit the formation of tensile stresses by promoting a more stable and controlled plastic deformation.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The current research focused on tool wear, Ra, chip morphology, and residual stress during milling of Carpenter® 20 under varied cutting strategies (cryo + NF-MQL, NF-MQL, and dry conditions) using a TiAlN-coated quenched tool. The conclusions reached from this research are drawn as follows:

The inclusion of 1 wt% Gr to corn oil reduced the contact angle (increased wettability) from 31.8 °C to 20.18 °C, increased the viscosity from 38 mPa.s to 51 mPa.s, and enhanced thermal conductivity from 0.152 W/mK to 0.183 W/mK. These improvements result in better surface wettability, stronger lubrication, and more efficient heat dissipation. Crater wear on the tool rack face was prominent under dry condition due to high thermal loads and chip adhesion. At higher Vc, coating delamination and nose damage increased. NF-MQL reduced adhesion and wear at low speeds but was less effective at higher thermal loads. Cryo + NF-MQL offered superior wear resistance through enhanced C/L effect. Dry cutting caused the highest Vb due to thermal softening and diffusion effects at 45 and 60 m/min, Vb reached 0.312 mm and 0.329 mm, respectively, under dry condition. Cryo + NF-MQL showed the best performance, limiting Vb to 0.1552 mm and 0.163 mm for 45 and 60 m/min, respectively, by maintaining lower temperatures and enhanced lubrication. The roughness results show a strong dependence on cutting environments. Dry cutting produces the highest Ra due to increased friction and tool wear. NF-MQL improved surface finish significantly, lowering Ra to 1.36 μm and 1.3 μm through enhanced lubrication and thermal conductivity. Cryo + NF-MQL achieved the best results with Ra of 1.24 μm and 1.15 μm owing to its superior cooling and tribo-film formation. 2D and 3D surface topography analysis confirmed that cryo + NF-MQL produced the smoothest surface with fewer peaks and valleys, Sa of 0.73 μm, followed by NF-MQL (1.08 μm) and dry cutting (1.79 μm). Cryo + NF-MQL produced thin chips due to enhanced thermal control and stable shear condition. Dry condition led to uneven serration, thick chips due to high thermal load, and no lubrication. NF-MQL produced moderate chip thickness and serration. Dry machining induces high tensile residual stress due to excessive heat and plastic deformation, compromising surface integrity. NF-MQL reduces these stresses significantly because of more uniform plastic deformation. Cryo + NF-MQL further lowers the residual stress by rapidly dissipating heat and refining the microstructure.
